plan.planning_summary: This portfolio tests three distinct strategy axes for a VIS-NIR dichroic beam splitter: (1) maximum layer count with quarter-wave initialization to exploit full manufacturing budget for band separation, (2) reduced layer count to test whether fewer layers with free optimization can match performance while improving manufacturability, and (3) non-quarter-wave thickness freedom to test whether deviating from classic DBR physics improves the transition sharpness at 45° incidence. All routes use TiO2/SiO2 on fused silica substrate at 45° incidence. The axes are genuinely distinct because they test different hypotheses about where the performance bottleneck lies: layer count, optimization freedom, or stack topology. Literature L01, L13, L15 directly motivate dichroic beam splitter design; L23 supports the optimization methodology; L32 addresses 45° incidence challenges.

routes.title: Maximum Layer Count Quarter-Wave DBR with Free Thickness Optimization
routes.scientific_hypothesis: A 24-layer TiO2/SiO2 quarter-wave stack initialized design, when thicknesses are freely optimized, will achieve higher visible reflectance and NIR transmittance than designs with fewer layers, because more interfaces provide greater spectral selectivity.
routes.design_principle: Distributed Bragg reflector physics: alternating high/low index layers at quarter-wave optical thickness create constructive interference for reflection in the stopband. More pairs deepen and widen the stopband. At 45° incidence, the effective optical thickness shifts, requiring thickness compensation.
